strengths: Valuable large-scale multimodal dataset (421,363 pairs) with precise temporal alignment and preservation of 4D meteorological structure, larger and more comprehensive than existing benchmarks
Well-motivated technical design with three interpretable plug-and-play modules (DTGF, TGS, TGCA) directly addressing temporal, spatial, and vertical dimensionality challenges in meteorological data
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with ablation studies demonstrating complementary module contributions and strong performance on several tasks (87.13% T/F, 72.37% MC-main accuracy)
Good interpretability through weight visualizations connecting model decisions to meteorological physics (e.g., sensitive pressure levels and temporal dynamics match domain expectations)
Novel application of multimodal LLMs to structured scientific data with potential to inspire similar approaches in other domains
weaknesses: Fundamental data-reality mismatch: uses meteorological data from 12 hours AFTER warning issuance for retrospective analysis, but claims applicability to real-time forecasting requiring predictions before events—critical limitation unaddressed
NSW task (National Severe Weather prediction) achieves only 2.1% score despite being the most operationally useful application, with no proposed solutions
Severe unmitigated class imbalance: snow storms (1.7% of data) achieve <6% accuracy; no sophisticated handling strategies (class weighting, focal loss) attempted
Geographic limitation to China only with no evaluation on other regions or climate zones; claims about 'severe weather event prediction' overstated

Missing domain-specific baselines: all comparisons against general-purpose vision-language models; no comparison with meteorology-specific forecasting, physics-informed methods, or NWP-based approaches

strengths: Valuable dataset contribution: MP-Bench provides 421,363 samples with precise temporal alignment, multiple task types, and preserved spatiotemporal resolution—addressing genuine gap in multimodal weather prediction resources
Physical consistency validation: Supplementary analysis demonstrates learned weights align with meteorological physics and CMA warning criteria, providing validation beyond typical ablations
Comprehensive experimental protocol: Proper year-wise train/test split, multiple baselines, thorough ablation studies on modules and temporal windows, and cross-regional generalization testing
Well-motivated technical design: Three complementary modules (DTGF, TGS, TGCA) address specific aspects of meteorological data processing with clear motivation
Reproducibility support: Extensive supplementary material with detailed hyperparameters, training settings, and QA examples
weaknesses: Significant venue mismatch: Paper addresses meteorological domain prediction rather than computer vision—core contributions orthogonal to CVPR's traditional focus on visual perception tasks; better suited for domain-specific or general ML venues

Critical performance gap on realistic task: NSW task (generating actual warning text) achieves only 2.1/5 score versus 87% for T/F—makes model unsuitable for operational deployment despite claimed applicability

Problematic NSW evaluation: Relies on GPT-4o as judge without expert meteorologist validation, no inter-rater studies, qualitative scoring rubric with ambiguity, and inconsistent scale (0-5 vs 0-100) compared to other tasks

Limited technical novelty: Proposed modules are straightforward applications of existing techniques (L2-norm gating, Gaussian masking, channel attention); novelty primarily in combination rather than fundamental innovation

Geographic and temporal limitations: Training exclusively from China (2023-2024 only—2 years), generalization tested on only 1,000 US samples; unclear if approach transfers across climate zones or longer horizons

Unaddressed data quality concerns: Training labels are human-issued warnings potentially encoding forecaster biases; no expert review of warning accuracy; 'normal weather' samples not validated to match true distribution
Missing critical comparisons: No comparison with specialized meteorological forecasting systems, actual NWP models, or text-only baselines; difficult to assess improvement over existing practice

Unclear distinction in data representation: Paper criticizes prior image-based approaches but still processes through vision-based MLLM encoders; fundamental limitation not clearly resolved or distinguished
Insufficient failure analysis: Limited case study showing errors in compound weather; no systematic analysis of error modes or proposed solutions; no comparison with human forecaster errors
Weak connection between modules and problem: Parallel fusion strategy and 12-hour window selection lack rigorous justification; unclear why these specific architectural choices versus alternatives
